scope_notice: This is a historical US-market case, not a historical SPCX case.

evidence.text: The administration announced a 25% tariff on imported cars and certain parts. The car tariff was scheduled to begin on 3 April; businesses with international supply chains faced a change in future import costs.

steps: uncertain import costs and supply chains
less predictable business profits and growth
possible_market_mechanism.explanation: Possible explanation: Tariffs can raise import costs and make future profits harder to predict. Businesses may delay investment while investors reassess growth and equity risk. Demand for safer bonds may rise, although inflation concerns can pull yields the other way.

evidence.text: The published estimate put fourth-quarter real GDP growth at a 2.4% annual rate, slower than the third quarter. It described a still-expanding economy before the coming trade-policy changes.

steps: support for company sales and earnings
growth support can compete with valuation pressure
possible_market_mechanism.explanation: Possible explanation: An expanding economy can support company sales. At the same time, resilient growth can reduce the urgency for rate cuts, so the effect on shares depends on the balance between earnings support and borrowing costs.

evidence.text: February PCE prices rose 0.3% over the month; excluding food and energy, prices rose 0.4% and were 2.8% above a year earlier. Investors had to weigh continuing inflation pressure alongside growth and trade-policy risks.

steps: bond yields and equity valuations may adjust
possible_market_mechanism.explanation: Possible explanation: Price releases influence expectations for central-bank interest rates. Persistent inflation can keep borrowing costs high; cooling inflation can ease that pressure. A price release alone does not establish why the whole market moved.

lessons.text: A tariff can raise a company's costs before it changes reported profits. Policy uncertainty can therefore move share prices ahead of earnings.
An economy can still be growing while investors worry about what comes next. GDP describes an earlier period; new policy risks can change expectations before they appear in the growth figures.
Inflation news affects both purchasing power and expected interest rates. A single price report does not determine the direction of the stock market.
